title: The 137.5° phyllotaxis angle results from a simple inhibition growth process

fields.label: Label
fields.value: The 137.5° phyllotaxis angle results from a simple inhibition growth process

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The near-universal 137.5° (golden-ratio) angle between successive plant organs is not an optimization found by natural selection but the inevitable result of a simple process where each new element forms where a chemical concentration is highest and depletes it nearby.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: And instead what I strongly suspect is that the patterns are just inevitable consequences of a rather simple process of growth not unlike one that was already discussed, at least in general terms, nearly a century ago.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 8, “Implications for Everyday Systems”; section “Growth of Plants and Animals” (from p. 400), p. 408. Scope: phyllotaxis and spiral arrangements of plant organs

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch08-21: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.58

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Phyllotactic angles and molecular perturbations are measurable, and public studies can test portions of the inhibitory mechanism. Existing data are scattered and do not cover the claimed universality. Similar predictions from rival models reduce causal discrimination.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Measure successive organ angles and inhibitory-field markers in shoot apical meristems, perturb the relevant transport or signaling process, and compare trajectories with the specified depletion model and optimization alternatives. Recovery of approximately 137.5 degrees from measured dynamics and predicted perturbation responses would support the mechanism.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Multiple inhibitory and mechanical models predict golden-angle phyllotaxis.

Near-universal and inevitable overstate known taxonomic and dynamical variation.

The chemical concentration in the claim is not uniquely specified.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The angle is a sharp prediction, and both the inhibition model and nonliving experiments that produce it are reproducible with public methods and published measurements. Those measurements are dispersed rather than deposited as one dataset, and photographs do not replace goniometry. The mechanism is testable now for well-studied plants; the further denial of any optimizing role for selection is not settled by the same evidence.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Measure divergence angles in a wide sample of plants and run the local-depletion model, testing whether it converges to about 137.5 degrees and whether physical or chemical inhibition experiments do the same without a fitness search. Convergence to that angle under inhibition, including in nonliving analogs, would support the growth mechanism; a different angle, or an angle that appears only when a shading optimum is imposed, would count against it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Showing that a growth rule yields the angle does not by itself prove that selection played no role in retaining it.

There is no single open archive of measured divergence angles across the plant kingdom.
